section.title: God Has Spoken by His Son
section.sectionRationale: The letter opens with a single, soaring sentence that sets the theme for everything that follows: God, who spoke in many pieces through the prophets, has now spoken His final and fullest word in a Son. Seven descriptions of the Son lift Him above every previous messenger and prepare the argument for His supremacy.
section.thesis: God's revelation reaches its climax in the Son, who is heir of all things, the agent of creation, the radiance of God's glory and the exact imprint of His nature, the sustainer of all things, and the one who, having purified sins, sat down at God's right hand.
section.frameNote: One sentence in two beats: the contrast between the old speaking through prophets and the final speaking in the Son; then a sevenfold portrait of who this Son is and what He has done.

units.label: God has spoken, at last, in a Son

verses.text: On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets.
But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son, whom He appointed {{kleronomos|heir}} of all things, and through whom He made the universe.

units.label: Who the Son is and what He has done

verses.text: The Son is the {{apaugasma|radiance}} of God’s glory and the exact {{charakter|representation}} of His {{hypostasis|nature}}, upholding all things by His powerful word. After He had provided purification for sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.
So He became as far superior to the angels as the name He has inherited is excellent beyond theirs.

kleronomos.gloss: An heir, one who receives an inheritance. The Son is appointed heir of all things: the whole created order is His rightful possession. What Adam lost and Israel foreshadowed, the Son inherits in full, and those united to Him become fellow heirs.

apaugasma.gloss: Radiance, the shining out of light from its source, as brightness streams from the sun. The Son is not a reflected or lesser light but the very radiance of God's glory, of one being with the Father, God shining forth as God.

charakter.gloss: The exact impress or stamp, as an engraving left by a seal or the image struck on a coin. The Son is the precise imprint of God's very being: to see Him is to see exactly what God is like.

hypostasis.gloss: Substance, essential nature, that which underlies and stands beneath appearance. The Son bears the exact imprint of God's own essence, sharing fully in the divine nature rather than merely resembling it.

basic.context: Hebrews begins without a normal greeting and plunges straight into its theme. For centuries God had spoken through prophets, a little at a time, in many forms: visions, laws, promises. Now, in these last days, He has spoken His final word in His Son. Everything the letter goes on to say about Jesus being greater than angels, Moses, and the old priesthood flows from this opening.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as the thesis statement of the whole letter. The point is not that the old revelation was false but that it was partial and preparatory; the Son is the full and final word. Seven phrases describe the Son, moving from His inheritance and role in creation to His deity, His sustaining power, His finished work, and His enthronement.
basic.originalLanguages: The Son is heir, klēronomos, of all things. He is the apaugasma, the radiance, of God's glory, and the charaktēr, the exact imprint, of God's hypostasis, His very nature. These words together confess that the Son is fully God, shining out from God and stamped with God's own being.
basic.typology: Every prophet who ever spoke for God was a partial foreshadowing of the one who is God's own Word. The purification for sins the Son provided fulfills the whole sacrificial system, and His sitting down fulfills what no priest under the law could ever do, for their work was never finished.
basic.christ: This is one of the highest portraits of Christ in Scripture. He is the eternal Son, the exact expression of God, the one through whom the universe was made and by whom it is held together, the one who purified sins and sat down at God's right hand. He is both the message and the messenger, God's final word to us.
basic.god: God is a speaking God who longs to be known. He did not stay silent, and He did not stop with the prophets; He gave His own Son. The Father appoints the Son heir, made the world through Him, and seats Him at His right hand, the place of highest honour and authority.
basic.crossReferences: John 1 says the Word was God and made all things. Colossians 1 calls the Son the image of the invisible God, in whom all things hold together. Psalm 110 seats the Lord at God's right hand.
basic.oneStory: The whole Bible is God speaking, and here that long conversation reaches its goal. The prophets pointed forward in fragments; the Son is the full and final word. From creation, through the cross, to the throne, the story runs to Him.

context.literary:
The opening of Hebrews is one long, balanced sentence in the Greek, verses 1 to 4, and it is built like a hinge. Its first half is shaped by contrast: long ago and in these last days, the fathers and us, the prophets and a Son. The second half turns to the Son Himself and piles up clauses about what He is and what He has done. Nothing in the New Testament begins more like a work of oratory, and the writer shows his skill in the first word. The Greek of verse 1 chains together words that begin with the same letter, polymeros and polytropos, which the BSB renders 'on many past occasions and in many different ways.' It sounds like a rolling, scattered revelation, a word given in pieces and by many routes, before the sentence arrives at a single speaker.

The main verb of the whole sentence is 'has spoken,' verse 2. Everything else hangs from it: the Son is heir, agent of creation, radiance, imprint, sustainer, purifier, and enthroned. This matters for how we read the sevenfold description. The list is not a free-standing creed. It tells us who has spoken. The Son is God's last word because of who He is.

The movement of the clauses is also deliberate. The first three describe the Son before and above time: appointed heir, creator, and the shining out of God's glory. The next two describe His present rule: He upholds all things. The last two turn to the cross and the throne: purification made, and then the sitting down. The sentence starts at creation, passes through the cross, and ends at the right hand. In a few lines it covers what the rest of Scripture takes whole books to tell.

Hebrews has no greeting and no author's name. It opens like a sermon, and later calls itself a 'word of exhortation,' Hebrews 13:22. Verses 1 to 4 set up the first section of the letter, the Son above the angels, which runs through chapter 2 with the first warning inside it.
context.historical:
The readers were Jewish believers who had come to Christ and were now being tempted to retreat. The letter mentions earlier sufferings, Hebrews 10:32-34, and a weariness that is leading some to neglect gathering together, Hebrews 10:25. A faith centred on one who had been crucified looked small beside the splendour of the temple, the priesthood and the law of Moses, which were ancient, visible and honoured.

The writer meets that pressure by beginning with God's speaking. For a Jewish hearer, God's revelation had come through Moses and the prophets. They were the great figures, and no one could set anything above them. The opening of Hebrews concedes at once that God truly spoke to the fathers in many ways, through visions, laws, histories and psalms. The question is whether that speech was complete. The answer is that it was never meant to be, and that the Son is the word the others were waiting for.

The phrase 'these last days' belongs to the Jewish expectation of the age to come. The prophets spoke of 'the latter days,' as in Isaiah 2:2 and Hosea 3:5, when God would finally act to restore His people and rule the nations. To say that those days have arrived in the Son is to tell the readers that they are not at the end of a fading tradition but at the start of the fulfilment. They are living in the very time the prophets longed to see, 1 Peter 1:10-12.

The language used of the Son would also have rung with familiar sounds. Jewish writers spoke of God's Wisdom as His agent in creation, Proverbs 8:22-31, and of the Word by which God made the heavens, Psalm 33:6 and Psalm 33:9. The writer takes those themes and says that all of it finds its meaning in one person, who is not an attribute of God or a created agent but the Son Himself.
context.canonical:
Hebrews 1:1-4 gathers threads from across the Bible and ties them to one person. The creation account supplies the pattern of God speaking and things coming to be, Genesis 1:3, and Psalm 33:6 says that by the word of the LORD the heavens were made. The Wisdom tradition gives the picture of one at God's side in creation, Proverbs 8:30. John's Gospel turns it into a confession: in the beginning was the Word, and all things were made through Him, John 1:1-3, and no one has seen God, but the Son 'has made Him known,' John 1:18.

The closest parallel in the New Testament is Colossians 1:15-17, where the Son is 'the image of the invisible God' and 'in Him all things hold together.' Paul and the writer of Hebrews describe the same Christ in nearly the same terms, one by the language of image and the other by the language of radiance and imprint. Philippians 2:6-11 supplies the other side: the one in the form of God who took the form of a servant and was then exalted. Hebrews 1:3 holds both halves in a single verse.

The last clause, the sitting down at God's right hand, takes up Psalm 110:1, the most quoted Old Testament verse in the New. Jesus Himself used it, Matthew 22:44, Peter preached it at Pentecost, Acts 2:33-36, and Paul sets it behind his teaching of Christ's reign, Ephesians 1:20-22. Hebrews returns to the image repeatedly, Hebrews 8:1, Hebrews 10:12 and Hebrews 12:2, so that these first verses are a preview of the book's whole argument.

Finally, verse 2 looks forward. The Son is 'heir of all things,' and the story of the Bible's last book is the story of the inheritance coming into His hands, Revelation 5:12 and Revelation 11:15.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer wants his readers to see that they have not been given less than their fathers had, but more, and that to turn back would be a step down and not a return to safety. His whole letter is a pastoral appeal to people tempted to quit, and he begins by changing what they are looking at. They had been staring at the cost of following Jesus, the shame and the loss. He turns their eyes to the one they follow.

He also intends to give a standard for reading the Old Testament. If God has spoken finally in a Son, then the earlier words are not to be thrown out but read in the light of Him. The prophets spoke truly, but they spoke about Him. That is why the letter that follows is full of quotations from the Psalms and the Law, and why it handles them confidently, as the voice of the Father and the Son talking to each other.

Finally, he intends to establish that listening to the Son is not optional. A word spoken by God in person carries weight in proportion to the speaker, as chapter 2 will say outright. The first verse is a doctrine and also a summons.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
These verses are declaration and not instruction. There is no command in them, and the temptation is to treat them as a list of statements to agree with. But in a letter built to hold people steady, a declaration is the foundation for every command that follows. The reader is not told to do anything yet; he is told who has spoken.

It is worth being careful about what is and is not being described. The passage says that God spoke by the prophets 'on many past occasions and in many different ways,' and that this speech was partial. It does not say the earlier revelation has ended or become false. What is described is a history of speaking that has now reached its goal. For us the lesson is that Scripture is read in the order God gave it, with the Son as its end, and that no later claim to a new revelation can stand beside Him as an equal.

The seven descriptions of the Son are also not a recipe to apply to ourselves. Believers are not heirs of all things in that way, nor sustainers of the world. They are, as later chapters will say, joint heirs and sharers, but those are different statements. Here the point is simply who He is.

debates.question: What does 'in these last days' mean?

views.label: The final era begun at Christ's first coming
views.case: The Greek phrase echoes the prophets' 'latter days,' Isaiah 2:2, and the New Testament treats the coming of Jesus as the start of that era, Acts 2:16-17, 1 Peter 1:20. The church lives in the last days already, between His first coming and His return.

views.label: The very end of the age, close at hand
views.case: Hebrews also speaks of the day approaching, Hebrews 10:25, and of the Lord coming 'in just a little while,' Hebrews 10:37, so some read the phrase as pointing to the nearness of the final consummation, with the Son's coming as the last act before it.

views.label: A simple contrast with the past
views.case: A minority read it as no more than 'recently' as opposed to 'long ago,' a plain time marker. The prophetic overtones of the wording make that reading thin.

debates.bearing: The first two views overlap more than they compete: the last days began with Christ and are being completed. In every case the Son's coming is the decisive moment, and nothing remains to wait for except His return.

debates.question: What is 'the name He has inherited,' verse 4?

views.label: The name 'Son'
views.case: The argument that follows in verses 5 to 14 begins with 'You are My Son,' and the contrast with angels turns on that title. The Son is called Son in a way no angel ever was.

views.label: The name 'Lord' or 'God'
views.case: Others point to Philippians 2:9-11, where the name above every name is the name of the Lord, and to the quotations in verses 8 to 10 where the Son is addressed as God and Lord.

views.label: The full dignity belonging to His enthroned person
views.case: Some say 'name' means rank and honour, so that it covers all the titles at once.

debates.bearing: All three lead to one conclusion, that the Son is no creature. The word 'inherited' is also important: the name is His by right of Sonship and not by promotion from a lower rank.

study.originalLanguages:
The prologue is dense with words that appear rarely, and a few choices in the English are worth looking at more closely.

The opening pair, polymeros and polytropos, are 'in many parts' and 'in many ways.' The first speaks of revelation given in fragments, a piece here and a piece there, the second of its variety of means: visions, dreams, law, history, poetry and symbol. The writer does not belittle these means. He says that they were many, and that the many are now answered by one.

In verse 2 the Greek says that God has spoken 'in Son,' en huio, with no article, and the BSB footnote gives 'Or in His Son.' The bare form puts the emphasis on the kind of speaker: not a prophet, not an angel, but one whose very nature is sonship. The verb 'has spoken' is in a tense that treats the speaking as one completed event with abiding result.

The heir, kleronomos, is the one who receives what belongs to the family. The footnote on 'the universe' says 'literally the ages,' aiones. The Son is the one through whom God made not only the physical cosmos but time itself, the ages in which history unfolds. The thought is not far from John 1:3.

Verse 3 is where the language turns most precise. The Son is the apaugasma of God's glory. The word can mean 'radiance,' light streaming out from a source, or 'reflection,' light thrown back by a mirror. Both fit the Son, but the context, with the Son as the maker and sustainer, makes radiance the better sense: the sun's light is not a thing apart from the sun. It appears only here in the New Testament. The second word, charakter, appears only here too, and comes from the stamp used to strike a coin, an engraved die that leaves its exact image in the wax. The BSB has 'exact representation.' Together they say that the Son is both inseparable from God, as brightness from fire, and an exact likeness of God, as impression from the seal. Fathers of the church later used the pair of images, light from light, against those who said the Son was a lesser being.

The word hypostasis, rendered 'nature,' is the underlying reality of something, what stands beneath. The same word is translated 'assurance' in both Hebrews 3:14 and Hebrews 11:1, which shows its range: the solid ground under a thing. The Son bears the very reality of God and not just an outward appearance.

The participle pheron, 'upholding,' does not mean holding up like a pillar that stays still. It carries the sense of bearing along, carrying something toward its goal. The Son carries the universe along 'by His powerful word,' the same kind of word as at the creation, the rhema of His power. Finally, the verb ekathisen, 'sat down,' is in a tense that points to a single past act, and it contrasts with Hebrews 10:11-12, where priests 'stand' day after day, but this Priest sat down.

typology.fulfillment: Moses spoke with God face to face, Numbers 12:6-8, yet he could say that God would raise up a prophet like him, to whom Israel must listen, Deuteronomy 18:15. Peter takes this as fulfilled in Jesus, Acts 3:22-23. The correspondence is of messenger to message: every prophet carried a piece of the word, and Jesus is the Word, John 1:14. The escalation is that He does not merely deliver God's message but is its content, and He speaks as Son and not as servant, Hebrews 3:5-6. The type falls short in that no prophet could be the word he spoke.

David's Lord is invited to sit at God's right hand until His enemies become a footstool, Psalm 110:1. Jesus used this verse to show that the Messiah is more than David's son, Matthew 22:41-45, and Peter says that David did not ascend into heaven, Acts 2:34-35. Hebrews 1:3 shows the Lord seated, Hebrews 10:12-13 shows Him waiting for the enemies to be placed beneath Him. David's own throne was an earthly shadow, and even Solomon, with all his glory, sat on a throne that would pass. The type falls short because every Davidic king died; this Son sits for ever.

typology.type: The Day of Atonement and the priest who sits
typology.fulfillment: On the Day of Atonement the high priest entered the Most Holy Place with blood and then left again, Leviticus 16:15-17, and no chair stood in the tabernacle, for the work was never done, Hebrews 10:11. In Christ the correspondence appears in the single phrase 'purification for sins' followed by 'sat down.' He offered Himself, Hebrews 9:11-14, and the work was finished, Hebrews 10:12-14. The escalation is from repeated shadow to once-for-all reality. The limit of the type is that the old priests offered another's blood; this Priest offered His own.

Proverbs 8:22-31 speaks of Wisdom beside God at the making of the world, rejoicing before Him. The New Testament does not call Jesus the figure of Proverbs 8 in so many words, so this is an echo and not a stated type. But Paul does call Christ the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24 and 1 Corinthians 1:30, and Colossians 1:15-17 uses the creation language directly. The correspondence is real, but the limit is that Proverbs personifies an attribute, while Hebrews names a person.

study.christ:
The prologue gives one of the fullest portraits of Christ in the New Testament, and each clause answers a different question.

Who is He in relation to the Father? He is the Son, and the radiance and exact imprint of God. He did not become God's Son at a point in time; the writer has just said that through Him God made the ages. The titles are not in tension with His humanity, which Hebrews insists on in chapter 2, but they come first. Before He was made like His brothers, He was the shining out of the Father's glory, John 17:5. To see Him is to see the Father, John 14:9, and this is why the writer can say that God has spoken in Him. His life is the speech.

What is He in relation to creation? The Son is both the one through whom the world was made and the one who now holds it together. Colossians 1:16-17 says that all things were created through Him and for Him and that in Him they hold together. The cosmos is not left to run by itself, and the same hand that formed it keeps it. For a church under pressure and a world that looked chaotic, that is a settling thought.

What has He done about sin? The central clause is easy to miss because it is so brief: 'After He had provided purification for sins.' Everything that Hebrews will say about priesthood, sacrifice and covenant stands behind those words. The one who upholds the universe stooped to deal with the stain of sin, and He did it Himself. The writer will not say how until later, but he places it here, between creation and the throne, where it belongs.

Where is He now? Seated. The posture speaks. No priest in the temple sat in the holy place, because the work could not be finished. Christ sat, because the sacrifice was complete, Hebrews 10:12. He sits at the right hand of 'the Majesty on high,' which is a Jewish way of avoiding God's name, and so shares the throne of God. Peter and Paul both speak of this exaltation, Acts 2:33 and Ephesians 1:20-22.

A guard against misuse is needed. The prologue is not Greek philosophy in Jewish dress. It does not build a theory of emanation or ask the reader to climb a ladder of being. It tells a story with a person at its heart, one who made, one who bore sin and one who reigns. The doctrine of the Trinity that the church later confessed grew out of statements like these, but the writer is not writing a creed. He is encouraging tired believers that the one they follow is what they hoped, and more.
study.god:
The first thing the passage shows about God is that He speaks. The living God is not silent or hidden behind His creation. He initiates, and every stage of redemptive history is His speaking, from the call of Abraham to the last prophet. He speaks in many ways because He is rich, and He speaks in parts because He is patient, building understanding over generations.

God is also a Father who has a Son. The prologue gives us the Father and the Son in a relationship that precedes the world: the Son is the one through whom He made the ages and to whom He gives all things. In this the writer is not describing two gods or two rivals. The Son shines out from the Father as light from a flame and is stamped with His being as an image from a die. The persons are distinct, and the God is one. The prologue does not use the word Trinity, and does not mention the Holy Spirit until chapter 2, but it shows the shape that the later church would need words for.

God is sovereign over history. The phrase 'in these last days' tells us that He moves time toward its goal, that the long period of partial revelation was a plan and not an accident, and that the fullness came when He decided it should. Galatians 4:4 says the same: 'when the time had fully come, God sent His Son.' The God of this passage does not react to events; He appoints an heir and brings about an inheritance.

God is the sustainer of all things, working through His Son. This is not the deist's absentee maker. The 'powerful word' by which the universe is carried is the same word that spoke it into being, Psalm 33:9, and it holds the stars and the seasons in place. It is also the word that speaks to the tired believers.

God is holy and also merciful. The writer says that purification for sins was provided and then places the Son on the throne. The holy God deals with sin by providing the remedy at His own cost, and the throne is not a place of terror for the cleansed. That is why this is the letter's foundation for its invitation, in chapter 4, to approach the throne of grace with confidence.

For worship, the response is attention. If God has spoken finally, the right posture of a believer is to listen, to read the Scriptures as the voice of the Son, and to refuse every substitute. The writer will say in chapter 12, 'See to it that you do not refuse Him who speaks,' Hebrews 12:25.

crossReferences.note: John names the divine speaker as the Word, who was with God and was God. Hebrews names the same person the Son and says God spoke through Him. The two writers approach from different sides, speech and sonship, and meet at a Person who stands before creation as its maker.

No one has seen God, but the Son 'has made Him known.' This is the reason Hebrews can say God has spoken by a Son. The invisible God became visible in the one who is Himself God and at the Father's side.

Paul's hymn calls the Son the image of the invisible God and holds that everything was made in Him, through Him and for Him. It is the closest parallel to Hebrews 1:2-3 and shows that both writers inherited a shared confession of Christ's work in creation and providence.

The hymn follows the same arc as the prologue: one who is in the form of God, who humbles Himself to death, and whom God exalts to the highest place. Hebrews 1:3 compresses this into two clauses, the purification for sins and the sitting down at the right hand.

The text behind the last phrase of verse 3. The Lord says to David's Lord, 'Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.' It is the most quoted verse of the Old Testament in the New, and Hebrews returns to it again and again.

By the word of the LORD the heavens were made. The Old Testament source of the idea that God creates by speaking, which Hebrews gathers into the Son: He who spoke the world into being is the same one through whom God spoke last and finally.

Looks back to the 'sat down' of 1:3. Priests stand day after day offering the same sacrifices that can never take away sins, but this Priest offered one sacrifice for all time and sat down. The phrase in verse 3 is the key to the whole contrast.

The closing warning of the letter takes up the opening word. 'See to it that you do not refuse Him who speaks.' The same God who spoke by the Son must be heard. The letter begins and ends with the same stress on speech.

Peter preaches that Jesus has been exalted to God's right hand and quotes Psalm 110:1 as proof. It shows that the enthronement in Hebrews 1:3 was part of the earliest apostolic message and not an invention of the letter's author.
When the time had fully come, God sent His Son. It matches 'in these last days' as a statement that the coming of the Son was timed by God, in the fullness of history and not at random.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with God speaking. 'Let there be light,' Genesis 1:3, and the world comes to be at His word. When humanity turned from Him in Genesis 3, God did not fall silent. He walked in the garden and asked, 'Where are you?', and the rest of the Old Testament is the story of that continued speaking: to Noah, to Abraham, to Moses at the burning bush and at Sinai, to the prophets in visions and to the psalmists in song. Each of these was a real word, and each looked beyond itself.

Hebrews 1:1-4 is the point where that long speaking arrives. The one who spoke at creation, Psalm 33:6, has now spoken in His own person. The thread that ran through the covenants, the promised seed of Genesis 3:15, the son given to Abraham, the king promised to David in 2 Samuel 7:12-14, finds its end in a Son who is also the radiance of God. The sacrifices that never finished the work, the kings who died, the prophets who passed away, are all gathered up and answered.

The prologue also places this moment on the arc of the whole story. The Son who is 'heir of all things' is the one who will receive what was lost in Eden. Adam was given dominion and lost it. In Hebrews 2:5-9 the writer will say that we do not yet see everything under man's feet, but we see Jesus, crowned. The recovery of the world has already begun, because its rightful heir has made purification for sins and sat down.

And it is still moving to its close. The word 'until' in Psalm 110:1 means that the Son is waiting for His enemies to be put beneath His feet, Hebrews 10:13. The Bible's last book shows the end: the throne of God and of the Lamb, Revelation 22:3, from which the new creation is governed, and a people who see His face. The God who spoke in many ways at the beginning will, at the end, be present with His people, Revelation 21:3. Between the first word and the last, there is one point where all the others meet, and the prologue names it: He has spoken to us by His Son.

quiz.q: How is God's speaking in the Son different from His speaking through the prophets?

options.text: The prophets spoke in part and in many ways; the Son is God's full and final word.
options.note: Verses 1 to 2 contrast the partial, varied prophetic word with the climactic word in the Son.

options.text: The prophets were false and only the Son is true.
options.note: The prophets were true but partial; the Son is the fuller revelation, not a correction of lies.

options.text: God had never spoken at all before the Son.
options.note: God did speak through the prophets; the point is that the Son is the final word.

options.text: There is no real difference between them.
options.note: The text draws a deliberate contrast between the former speaking and the Son.

quiz.q: What does it mean that the Son is the radiance of God's glory and the exact imprint of His nature?

options.text: He is fully God, shining out from God and bearing God's very being.
options.note: The words radiance and exact imprint confess the Son's full deity.

options.text: He is the greatest of created beings, reflecting God's light.
options.note: He is not a creature reflecting light but the radiance itself, of one being with God.

options.text: He merely resembles God in character.
options.note: He does share God's character, but the terms mean far more: He is the exact imprint of God's essence.

options.text: He is a symbol of God's glory only.
options.note: He is not a symbol but God shining forth in person.

quiz.q: What is the significance of the Son sitting down at the right hand of the Majesty?

options.text: His work of purifying sins is finished, and He reigns in supreme honour.
options.note: Sitting down signals a completed work and enthronement, unlike the ever-standing priests.

options.text: He was tired and needed rest.
options.note: The sitting is enthronement and completion, not fatigue.

options.text: He took a lower place to serve the angels.
options.note: The right hand is the highest place; He is above the angels.

options.text: He is waiting to finish a work still incomplete.
options.note: The purification was already provided; He then sat down, His atoning work complete.

quiz.q: What roles does the Son have in relation to creation?

options.text: The universe was made through Him, and He upholds all things by His word.
options.note: He is both the agent of creation and its sustainer.

options.text: He watches creation from a distance without involvement.
options.note: He actively made and now sustains all things.

options.text: He created only the spiritual world, not the physical.
options.note: He made the whole universe, not a part.

options.text: He made all things but left them to run on their own.
options.note: He not only made all things but continually upholds them.

questions: God has spoken His final word in His Son. How does that shape where you go to hear from God, and how you treat the words of Jesus?
The Son is the exact imprint of God's nature. When you want to know what God is really like, do you look first to Jesus?
The Son upholds all things by His powerful word. What does it steady in you to know that the one who died for you also holds the universe together?
He provided purification for sins and then sat down. How does a finished work of cleansing free you from trying to cleanse yourself?
The Son is heir of all things. What would change if you lived as a fellow heir with Christ rather than as an anxious owner of your own small kingdom?

translationNotes.note: The phrase rendered 'the universe' is literally 'the ages', which can carry the sense of the whole created order across time; the Son is the agent of all that God made.
'Exact representation' renders charaktēr, the impress left by an engraving tool or seal; the Son is the precise stamp of God's own being, not an approximation.
'Nature' renders hypostasis, the underlying substance or essence; later theology used this word family in defining the persons of the Trinity.
